propositions.text: Claimants are citizens of China seeking refugee protection under IRPA ss 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: XXXXX and her minor daughter, XXXXX, citizens of the People's Republic of China (China), claim refugee protection pursuant to ss 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The claimants, Chinese citizens, seek refugee protection under IRPA ss 96 and 97(1), as stated by the applicant.

propositions.text: The principal claimant was appointed designated representative for her 17-year-old daughter at hearing.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant was appointed as the designated representative for her daughter, XXXXX who was seventeen years old at the time of the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The principal claimant was designated representative for her 17-year-old daughter at the hearing, as found by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: The principal claimant makes allegations in support of the refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant (henceforth referred to as the claimant) alleges the following:

paragraphs.summary: The principal claimant alleges facts supporting the refugee claim, as submitted by the applicant.

propositions.text: Claimant's husband was killed in 2006; husband's family focused on money, pressured claimant for funds and visas.
propositions.quote: The claimant's husband came to Canada as a skilled worker and was granted permanent resident status. Tragically, he was killed by a car while riding his bicycle to work on XXXXX, 2006. When the claimant learned of the death, she was distraught. When the claimant invited her husband's family to discuss the funeral arrangements, all they were interested in was discussing her husband's financial situation and whether he had purchased life insurance. They also wanted her to borrow money from her company for plane tickets and the funeral, which the claimant could not do. Instead, the claimant borrowed money from her relatives, friends and co-workers. One of her husband's brothers, XXXXX, wanted her to pay for his trip for the funeral in Canada, as his family had no money. On XXXXX, 2006, the claimant was granted a visa to come to Canada while XXXXX visa was refused. The brother-in-law did not want them to go until he could obtain his visa, no matter how long it took. When the claimant accompanied her daughter to obtain her visa, XXXXX tried to stop them from entering the embassy. They eventually managed to obtain the visa. The claimant's father-in-law came one day with his other son, XXXXX, and insisted that he had expected his eldest son to take care of him, but that since he is dead, the claimant had to give him the $250,000 compensation money and money from donations and had to buy a house for him. XXXXX insisted that if the claimant did not give them the money, he would take her passport and not return it. He pushed the claimant to the edge of the bed and kept yelling at her.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges her husband died in 2006; his family pressured her for money and visas, including threats and physical intimidation, as submitted by the applicant.

propositions.text: Claimant received call from CSA president about husband's family demanding funds and threatening to prevent claimants leaving China.
propositions.quote: On XXXXX, 2006, the claimant received a call from the president of the Canadian Shandong Association (CSA). The CSA had raised money for the claimants' trip and funeral costs. The president informed her that XXXXX had contacted her and asked that the CSA obtain a visa for his father and that the donated funds be sent to his father and his family. XXXXX said that he would not allow the claimants to leave China unless the CSA guaranteed that the funds would go to the claimant's husband's family. The president advised them to leave their home immediately, which they did the following morning.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges CSA president informed her husband's family demanded funds and threatened to prevent their departure, as submitted by the applicant.

propositions.text: Upon arrival in Canada, claimant learned husband's family threatened harm and sought their address.
propositions.quote: When the claimant arrived in Canada, she learned that her husband's family were searching for the claimant and making threats that they would break their legs and even kill them unless they got the money. The claimant's father-in-law kept sending e-mails to the CSA asking for money. Also, he twice called the president asking about the claimants and trying to get their address. He said that he would get a visa and come to Canada to find the claimants.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges husband's family threatened harm and sought their address after arrival in Canada, as submitted by the applicant.

propositions.text: Claimants received insurance and donations; husband's family disputes amounts and demands money.
propositions.quote: The claimants received an insurance payment in the amount of $41,000. They also received $69,000 in donations. There is a claim before the courts which has not been settled. Her husband's family does not believe that the claimant has not received a huge settlement of $250,000 and keep asking for money.

paragraphs.summary: The claimants received insurance and donations; husband's family disputes amounts and demands money, as submitted by the applicant.

propositions.text: Claimant fears harm from husband's family and lack of police protection if returned to China.
propositions.quote: The claimant fears that her husband's family may cripple or even kill them if they go back to China. The claimant feels that she cannot move to another area of China because she could not obtain a resident registration without property or a job. She also fears that her husband's family would easily find them. The claimant also fears that the police and authorities in China would not help them as they would regard the case as merely a family disagreement. They would only intervene if something serious were to happen.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant fears harm from husband's family and no police protection if returned to China, as submitted by the applicant.

propositions.text: Claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I determine that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court determines the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: Claimants' identities are established by testimony and documentation.
propositions.quote: The claimants' identities are established by their testimony and the documentation filed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants' identities established by testimony and documentation.

propositions.text: Court aware of interpreter difficulties and considered Gender Guidelines in this case.
propositions.quote: In arriving at my decision, I have been aware of the difficulties faced by a claimant in providing testimony through an interpreter in the unfamiliar milieu of a Canadian hearing room. I have also considered the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines in considering the facts of this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes interpreter difficulties and considers Gender Guidelines in deciding the case.

propositions.text: Whether there is nexus to grounds under s. 96 definition for persecution, including gender-based persecution.
propositions.quote: The determinative factor is whether there is nexus to any of the grounds under the definition of s. 96. Counsel has argued that the claimants are being persecuted because of their gender as they belong to a special social group of females fearing domestic violence.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue of nexus to s. 96 grounds, including gender-based persecution, as argued by counsel.

propositions.text: Claimants are not persecuted because of gender; minor claimant suffered discrimination, not persecution.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants are not being persecuted because of their gender. The minor claimant has testified that she was never treated well by her father's family because she is a girl and that they did not treat her very nicely or ignored her. There was no other evidence of mistreatment. I, therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that what the minor claimant suffered was discrimination and not persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants are not persecuted due to gender; minor claimant suffered discrimination only.

propositions.text: Claimant did not suffer past persecution, only discrimination; one incident of physical aggression was for extortion, not gender.
propositions.quote: I also find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant did not suffer persecution in the past, but only discrimination. The claimant testified that she did not have good relations with her husband's family because they were disappointed that she and her husband did not have a son. She and her husband had decided not to jeopardize their jobs and positions in having a second child, which was contrary to the Chinese One Child policy and they also did not want to get rid of their daughter in order to have a son. The claimant also testified that her husband had been supporting his father and his two brothers' families, who had lost their jobs due to the one child policy. The claimant gave no evidence that she was persecuted in the past by her family because of her gender. The claimant testified that there was one incident after her husband's death when her brother-in-law pushed her and tried to take her passport. The claimant did not say she was injured. The claimant did not give her passport to her in-laws. I find that had her brother-in-law and father-in-law wanted to take her passport they could have overpowered her, but they did not. Even in regard to this incident, I do not find that the physical actions were because of the claimant's gender but because the claimant's in-laws wanted to achieve their goal of guaranteeing that they received money they felt was due them.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant suffered past discrimination, not persecution; physical aggression was extortion-related, not gender-based.

propositions.text: Threats from husband's family are for extortion, not because claimants are female members of a social group.
propositions.quote: The question is whether the claimant would be persecuted by her husband's family because of her gender if she returns to China. The claimant testified that she tried to involve her husband's family in planning her husband's funeral. Instead of receiving sympathy, her in-laws were only concerned about going to the funeral themselves and getting life insurance money and donated money raised for the claimant. The claimant's brother-in-law tried to prevent her and her daughter from leaving China until he could get a visa. Later, the claimant's father in law tried to get the CSA that had raised money for the claimants to guarantee that they would remit half of the money to him. The claimant did not adduce any evidence whether her husband's family has any entitlement to this money under China's succession laws. She was specifically asked at the hearing if she knew if her in-laws had any legal entitlement to the money from her husband's estate. The claimant replied that she does not know and did not inquire about any entitlement they may have. If they do not, then what the family is attempting to do is to extort money from the claimant by threatening her and her daughter. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that if her husband's family is threatening them, it is not because they are female members of a particular social group, but because they want to obtain the money, some of which they may or may not be entitled to.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds threats are extortion-related, not due to claimants' gender or social group membership.

propositions.text: Claimants do not belong to a social group of women suffering domestic violence; fears relate to extortion, not domestic violence.
propositions.quote: I also find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants do not have membership in a social group of women suffering domestic violence. The claimants never adduced any evidence that they suffered any persecution within the family because of their relationship to family members, only discrimination. I have already found that what the claimants fear is persecution because of possible extortion and not domestic violence because of their relationship within the family.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants are not members of a domestic violence social group; fears relate to extortion, not domestic violence.

propositions.text: Whether threats from husband's family are genuine and likely to be acted upon.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that her husband's family has threatened to break their legs and even kill them if they do not hand over the large amount of life insurance and other moneys to which they feel they are entitled. However, the question remains whether these threats were genuine or whether they were empty threats uttered in the heat of the moment and whether they would be acted upon.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue whether threats from husband's family are genuine and likely to be acted upon.

propositions.text: Claimants arrived in Canada in 2006, claimed refugee status in 2008, and pursued H&C and judicial review applications.
propositions.quote: The claimants arrived in Canada in XXXXX 2006 and made their refugee claims in October 2008, some two and a half years after arrival. The claimants made every attempt to stay in Canada. Their application for a visitor's visa extension was refused. The claimant testified that it was her late husband's intention to bring her and her daughter to Canada and that he was saving money for that purpose. The minor claimant also indicated that she wanted to fulfill her father's dream by remaining in Canada and obtaining an education in Canada. The claimants made an application for Permanent Residency based on Humanitarian and Compassionate (H&C) grounds, but that application was refused. The reasons stated for pursuing the H&C application is that the claimants wished to stay in Canada because that was their dream and because their application for compensation is still before the courts and because the claimants would have problems re-establishing themselves after returning to China. The claimants applied for judicial review of that decision, but were unsuccessful. At no time during the H&C application did the claimants indicate that they were fearful of returning home to China because of the threats of their husband/father's family.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes claimants arrived in 2006, claimed refugee status in 2008, pursued H&C and judicial review, but never indicated fear of husband's family threats.

propositions.text: Claimants lacked subjective fear of persecution; did not disclose fear during H&C application despite legal advice.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that the Immigration officer who interviewed them suggested they make a refugee claim. The claimant further testified that up to that point she was unaware that she could make a refugee claim. I do not accept this explanation as the claimants had legal advice in reference to their H&C application and appeal and would have, on the balance of probabilities, been advised of their options. I find, therefore, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants lacked subjective fear.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants lacked subjective fear and did not disclose fear during H&C application despite legal advice.

propositions.text: Whether claimants have rebutted presumption of state protection despite threats from husband's family.
propositions.quote: I find that the determinative issue in this case is whether the claimants have rebutted the presumption of state protection. Even if the claimant's husband's family has the intention to harm the claimants, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants have not provided clear and convincing proof that state protection would not be available to them.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the key issue is whether claimants rebutted presumption of state protection; they have not done so.

propositions.text: There is a presumption that a state can protect its citizens except in complete state breakdown.
propositions.quote: There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens except in situations where the state is in a state of complete breakdown.

propositions.text: To rebut presumption, claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of state's inability to protect absent state's admission.
propositions.quote: To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national.

propositions.text: Effectiveness of protection is relevant, but test is whether protection offered is adequate.
propositions.quote: While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration, the test is whether the protection offered is adequate.

propositions.text: Evidence of inadequate state protection must be reliable, probative, and satisfy balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The evidence that state protection is not adequate must be reliable and probative and it must also satisfy me, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection is inadequate.

propositions.text: Claimant must approach state for protection if it might be reasonably forthcoming.
propositions.quote: The claimant must approach the state for protection, providing that state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.

propositions.text: State in effective control with authority and efforts to protect means failure to always protect is insufficient to claim lack of protection.
propositions.quote: Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to justify a claim that the victims are unable to avail themselves of protection.

propositions.text: Imperfection of state protection does not prove state's inability to protect citizens.
propositions.quote: The fact that state protection is not perfect does not constitute clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens, since no state can guarantee the protection of all its citizens at all times.

propositions.text: Local policing failures do not equal lack of state protection unless part of broader pattern of inability.
propositions.quote: Local failures to provide effective policing do not amount to a lack of state protection unless they are part of a broader pattern of the state's inability to provide protection.

propositions.text: Burden of proof on claimant increases with state's level of democracy.
propositions.quote: The burden of proof that rests on the claimant increases with the level of democracy of the state in question.

propositions.text: More democratic a state, more claimant must exhaust all options to show protection not forthcoming.
propositions.quote: The more democratic a state is, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all course of action open to them to demonstrate state protection was or would not be forthcoming.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the legal test for state protection, burden of proof, and adequacy of protection, citing relevant principles and standards.

propositions.text: China is not a democracy but government rules the country through laws and practice.
propositions.quote: Clearly, China is not a democracy. On the other hand, through its laws and practice, there is little doubt that the government of China rules the country.

propositions.text: China has law enforcement structure and ability to provide protection if prioritized.
propositions.quote: If the government determines to provide state protection, it has the law enforcement structure and ability to do so, to whatever extent it might prioritize the issue.

propositions.text: China has functioning judiciary and police force; state protection is element of Chinese society and legal system per Xue case.
propositions.quote: China has a functioning judiciary and police force. State protection has been determined to be an element of Chinese society and legal system in the oft-cited case of Xue.

propositions.text: Claimant must try to access available protection, especially as persecution is not by state and state combats domestic abuse and crime.
propositions.quote: The claimant must do what she can to access the available protection, particularly as the alleged persecution in this case is not at the hands of the state and the state is making efforts to combat serious domestic abuse as well as criminality.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds China is not democratic but has functioning state protection and claimant must try to access it, especially as persecution is non-state.

propositions.text: Claimants' claim is not appropriately based on a Convention ground.
propositions.quote: I have found above that the claimants' claim is not appropriately based on a Convention ground.

propositions.text: Country documents show some state protection exists for victims of serious domestic violence in China.
propositions.quote: Based upon the country documents, there is a level of state protection for the victims of serious domestic violence in China.

propositions.text: Violence against women is serious problem in China but steps are being taken to improve situation for abused spouses.
propositions.quote: Country documentation indicates that violence against women continues to be a serious problem in China. China is taking steps to improve the situation for abused spouses.

propositions.text: Claimants' fear relates to money issue, not continuing persecution; many aid programs likely not applicable but available.
propositions.quote: The claimants' fear of domestic violence is not of a continuing persecution but is specifically related to the one issue in regard to the money the claimants may or may not obtain. Most of the programs set up to aid women suffering domestic abuse in China, are therefore likely not applicable to the claimants, although they would still be able to use the services.

propositions.text: China has shelters, legal aid, police booths for domestic violence complaints; no national law criminalizing domestic violence but other laws provide mediation and penalties.
propositions.quote: For example, there are a growing number of shelters in China available for victims of domestic abuse, legal aid service centers and special police booths for domestic violence complaints. Although there is no national law criminalizing domestic violence, the criminal law, marriage law, and other laws on public security provide for mediation and administrative penalties in cases of domestic violence.

propositions.text: Claimants could use these protections and legal system if necessary.
propositions.quote: The claimants could avail themselves of these avenues of protection, if necessary, while seeking redress through the legal system.

propositions.text: Claimant has not provided relevant, reliable, convincing evidence that state protection in China is inadequate for threats from husband's family.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant has not adduced relevant, reliable and convincing evidence which satisfies me, the trier of fact, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection available in China to the claimants from the threats of their husband's/father's family, is inadequate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds some state protection exists for domestic violence victims in China and claimant failed to prove protection inadequate for threats from husband's family.

propositions.text: Claimant made no attempts to seek state protection while in China.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant made no attempts to seek state protection while in China.

propositions.text: Claimant was distressed over husband's death and focused on reaching Canada for funeral.
propositions.quote: I accept that the claimant was extremely distressed because of the death of her husband and was focused on reaching Canada to deal with her husband's death and funeral.

propositions.text: Claimant has been in Canada four years and could have reported threats to Chinese government via family or embassy.
propositions.quote: The claimant, however, has been in Canada for four years and therefore had the opportunity to report the threats from her husband's family to the Chinese government through her own family who remain in China or through the Chinese embassy or consulate and to seek their advice.

propositions.text: Claimant submitted photo with Chinese consul in Canada.
propositions.quote: The claimant even submitted a photograph of herself with the Chinese consul in Canada.

propositions.text: Claimant has not informed herself of Chinese succession laws regarding husband's estate claims.
propositions.quote: In addition, the claimant has testified that she has not informed herself of the Chinese succession laws to see if her husband's family has any legitimate claims to any money due to her husband's estate.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, claimant has not shown state protection is unavailable to her and daughter.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has not shown that state protection is not available to her and her daughter.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant made no attempts to seek state protection in China and has not shown protection is unavailable to her and daughter.

propositions.text: Claimant is intelligent, well-educated, had responsible job in China, and could re-establish herself there.
propositions.quote: The claimant is an intelligent, well-educated woman who had a responsible job in China. I would expect that the claimant could re-establish herself in China.

propositions.text: Claimant's family lives three hours from in-laws; claimant testified she could not move where in-laws could not find her.
propositions.quote: Apparently, her own family lives a three hour drive from her in-laws and that is where the claimants resided before coming to Canada. The claimant testified that she could not move anywhere in China where her in-laws could not find her.

propositions.text: Claimant testified sister-in-law's two brothers are PSB members who would help husband's family locate claimants due to desperation for money.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that her sister-in-law had two brothers who were members of the Public Security Bureau (PSB) and that they would help her husband's family to locate the claimants even if they moved to a different part of the country.

propositions.text: Claimant's belief that PSB officials would help husband's family is mere speculation.
propositions.quote: When the claimant was asked how she knew that they would help to locate her and daughter, she replied that they would do so because her husband's family is desperate for money. I find that this is mere speculation on the part of the claimant.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, claimants could relocate elsewhere in China to avoid alleged persecutors.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants could relocate in a different part of the country to be away from their alleged persecutors.

propositions.text: No evidence that PSB officials could prevent claimant from obtaining protection.
propositions.quote: The claimant also presented no evidence that these two PSB officials, one of whom works in an unnamed prison, could prevent the claimant from obtaining protection.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, husband's family lacks means to effectively block state protection.
propositions.quote: I do not conclude, based on the claimant's evidence and on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's husband's family has the means to effectively block state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's speculation about PSB officials helping husband's family is unsupported and claimants could relocate to avoid persecutors.

propositions.text: Elements to establish claim under s.97(1) IRPA differ from those under s.96 IRPA; s.96 claim not determinative of s.97 claim.
propositions.quote: The elements necessary to establish a claim under s. 97 (1) of the IRPA are not identical to those necessary to establish whether a person is a Convention refugee under s. 96 of the IRPA. A determination of a refugee claim under s. 96 of the IRPA, is not necessarily determinative of a claim under subsection 97 (1) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: In this case, whether claim framed under s.96 or s.97 IRPA, state protection is available to claimants.
propositions.quote: However, in the case at hand, whether the claim is framed under s. 96 or s. 97 of the IRPA, I find that there is state protection available to the claimants.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.97 and s.96 IRPA claims differ but finds state protection available to claimants under either.

propositions.text: State protection is available to claimants; no more than mere possibility of persecution or risk of torture, death, or cruel treatment if returned to China.
propositions.quote: I have concluded that state protection is available to the claimants. As a result, I am of the opinion that there is not more than a mere possibility that, should the claimants return to China, they would face persecution or, on the balance of probabilities, be in danger of torture or at risk to their lives or at risk of being subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes state protection is available and claimants face no more than mere possibility of persecution or risk if returned.

propositions.text: Claimants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection; claims rejected by Refugee Protection Division.
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, I conclude that the claimants are not Convention refugees and not persons in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects their claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects claimants' claims, finding they are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
